title: History Detective
teaches: Read a famous US market fall since 2000 like a detective: how deep it went, how long it took, what set it off and what came after.

facts.quote: The Great Recession began in December 2007 and ended in June 2009, which makes it the longest recession since World War II.
facts.claim: The recession behind the 2007-09 bear market ran from December 2007 to June 2009.

facts.quote: the S&P 500 index fell 57 percent from its October 2007 peak to its trough in March 2009.
facts.claim: The S&P 500 fell 57% from its October 2007 peak to its March 2009 trough.

facts.quote: Home prices fell approximately 30 percent, on average, from their mid-2006 peak to mid-2009
facts.claim: US home prices fell about 30% on average from mid-2006 to mid-2009.

facts.quote: This decline in home prices helped to spark the financial crisis of 2007-08, as financial market participants faced considerable uncertainty about the incidence of losses on mortgage-related assets.
facts.claim: Falling home prices helped spark the 2007-08 financial crisis, through losses on mortgage-related assets.

facts.quote: In September, Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, and the next day the Federal Reserve provided support to AIG
facts.claim: In September 2008 Lehman Brothers went bankrupt, and the next day the Fed supported AIG.

facts.quote: Temporary repairs to infrastructure were not completed until early the following week, and trading on the New York Stock Exchange did not resume until Monday, September 17.
facts.claim: After the September 11, 2001 attacks, NYSE trading did not resume until Monday, September 17.

facts.quote: the committee determined that a trough in business activity occurred in the US economy in November 2001. The trough marks the end of the recession that began in March 2001
facts.claim: The NBER dates the 2001 recession from March 2001 to November 2001.

facts.quote: July 17, 2003 CAMBRIDGE July 17 -- The Business Cycle Dating Committee of the National Bureau of Economic Research met yesterday.
facts.claim: The NBER announced the November 2001 trough on July 17, 2003, about 20 months after it.

facts.quote: CAMBRIDGE September 20, 2010 - The Business Cycle Dating Committee of the National Bureau of Economic Research met yesterday by conference call.
facts.claim: The NBER announced the June 2009 trough on September 20, 2010.

facts.quote: the committee determined that a trough in business activity occurred in the US economy in June 2009.
facts.claim: The NBER dates the end of the 2007-09 recession to June 2009.

facts.quote: Cambridge, July 19, 2021 - The Business Cycle Dating Committee of the National Bureau of Economic Research maintains a chronology of the peaks and troughs of US business cycles.
facts.claim: The NBER announced the April 2020 trough on July 19, 2021.

facts.quote: The committee has determined that a trough in monthly economic activity occurred in the US economy in April 2020.
facts.claim: The NBER dates the end of the 2020 recession to April 2020.

facts.quote: most major equity indexes reached record highs in March, with the Wilshire 5000 rising 6-3/4 percent above its 1999 year-end level and the Nasdaq soaring 24 percent
facts.claim: Most major US stock indexes, the Nasdaq among them, hit record highs in March 2000.

facts.quote: Equity prices fell from these highs during the spring, with a particularly steep drop in the Nasdaq, as investors grew more concerned about the lofty valuations of some sectors and the prospect of higher interest rates.
facts.claim: From spring 2000 stocks fell from those highs, the Nasdaq steeply, as investors worried about lofty valuations and higher rates.

facts.quote: In 2002, the United States economy extended the upturn in activity that began in late 2001.
facts.claim: The US economy kept growing through 2002, after the upturn that began in late 2001.

facts.quote: Over the spring and summer, accounting scandals, widespread warnings about near-term corporate profitability, and heightened geopolitical tensions intensified the slide in stock prices.
facts.claim: In spring and summer 2002, accounting scandals, profit warnings and geopolitical tension deepened the stock slide.

facts.quote: By early October, equity indexes sank to their lowest levels since the spring of 1997
facts.claim: By early October 2002, US stock indexes were at their lowest since spring 1997.

facts.quote: Share prices turned around in late October, as the third-quarter corporate earnings reports were not as weak as investors had originally feared.
facts.claim: Stocks turned up in late October 2002 when third-quarter earnings came in better than feared.

facts.quote: Equity markets fell sharply in late July and early August in response to concerns about the European crisis, the U.S. debt ceiling debate, and a possible slowdown in global growth.
facts.claim: In late July and early August 2011 US stocks fell sharply on Europe's crisis, the US debt-ceiling fight and fears of slower global growth.

facts.quote: Standard and Poor's (S&P), which had put the U.S. long-term sovereign credit rating on credit watch negative in June, downgraded that rating from AAA to AA+ following the passage of the act
facts.claim: In August 2011, S&P cut the US long-term credit rating from AAA to AA+.

facts.quote: Equity prices roughly retraced these losses during the fourth quarter of 2011 and early 2012
facts.claim: Stocks roughly won back those 2011 losses by the fourth quarter of 2011 and early 2012.

facts.quote: broad measures of U.S. equity prices have decreased notably, on net, as concerns about the foreign economic outlook appeared to weigh on risk sentiment and the outlook for corporate earnings growth
facts.claim: From mid-2015 into early 2016, US stocks fell notably on worries about the economic outlook abroad.

facts.quote: Stock prices for companies in the energy and basic materials sectors dropped sharply, reflecting the continued fall in oil and other commodity prices.
facts.claim: Energy and materials stocks dropped sharply as oil and other commodity prices kept falling.

facts.quote: These developments, which contributed to intensified uncertainty about China's exchange rate policy and the prospects for its economy, fostered episodes of global market turbulence
facts.claim: Uncertainty about China's currency policy and its economy set off bouts of global market turbulence in 2015-16.

facts.quote: At 9:30, SPY opened for regular trading hours at 5.2% below its previous day's close and then further declined to a daily low of 7.8% by 9:35.
facts.claim: On August 24, 2015 the S&P 500 fund SPY opened 5.2% below Friday's close and was down 7.8% by 9:35.

facts.quote: By 9:40, SPY recovered past its opening price and eventually closed down 4.2%.
facts.claim: By 9:40 SPY was back above its open, and it closed the day down 4.2%.

facts.quote: declined to its limit down price of 5% below the previous trading day's closing price and was paused for trading from 9:25 to 9:30.
facts.claim: Before the open, E-Mini S&P 500 futures fell to their 5% limit-down price and paused from 9:25 to 9:30.

facts.quote: The stop price is not the guaranteed execution price for a stop order. The stop price is a trigger that causes the stop order to become a market order.
facts.claim: A stop price is a trigger that turns the order into a market order, not a guaranteed fill price.

facts.quote: if markets are volatile and stock prices are changing rapidly, your stop order may be executed at a price that's significantly different from your stop price.
facts.claim: In fast markets a stop order can fill far from its stop price.

facts.quote: Rapid price movement during a short period of time could trigger a stop order. Due to market volatility, the stock might later rebound and resume trading at its prior price level.
facts.claim: A short, sharp move can trigger a stop, and the price may rebound afterwards.

facts.quote: Generally, a bear market occurs when a broad market index falls by 20% or more over at least a two-month period.
facts.claim: Generally, a bear market is a fall of 20% or more in a broad index over at least two months.
The S&P 500 closed at 2,930.75 on September 20, 2018, its highest close in the cited series before April 2019.
The S&P 500 closed at 2,351.10 on December 24, 2018, the lowest close in the cited series.
On April 23, 2019 the S&P 500 closed at 2,933.68, its first close above 2,930.75 since September 20, 2018 (every close between is in the cited series).
The S&P 500 closed at 4,796.56 on January 3, 2022, the peak before the 2022 bear market.
The S&P 500 closed at 3,666.77 on June 16, 2022, its lowest close of 2022 up to that day.
The S&P 500 closed at 4,305.20 on August 16, 2022, the highest close between June 16 and October 12, 2022.
The S&P 500 closed at 3,577.03 on October 12, 2022, the lowest close in the cited series, below the June 16 close.
On January 19, 2024 the S&P 500 closed at 4,839.81, its first close above 4,796.56 since January 3, 2022.
The Nasdaq Composite closed at 5,048.62 on March 10, 2000, its highest close in the cited series before April 2015.
The Nasdaq Composite closed at 1,114.11 on October 9, 2002, the lowest close in the cited series.
On April 23, 2015 the Nasdaq Composite closed at 5,056.06, its first close above its March 10, 2000 close (every close between is in the cited series).

facts.quote: Prior bear markets for the S&P 500 Start date End date Start price End price Months S&P 500 % change
facts.claim: S&P Dow Jones Indices' table lists each S&P 500 bear market's start and end date, prices, length in months and % change.
S&P DJI: the 2000-02 bear ran from March 24, 2000 (1,527.46) to October 9, 2002 (776.76), 30.5 months, down 49.1%.
S&P DJI: the 2007-09 bear ran from October 9, 2007 (1,565.15) to March 9, 2009 (676.53), 17 months, down 56.8%.

facts.quote: So, how does S&P Global define the end of a bear market? When the index reaches its low and later rises by 20%. Unfortunately for investors, that can only be known in hindsight.
facts.claim: S&P DJI marks a bear market's end at the low, once the index later rises 20%, so the end is only known in hindsight.

facts.quote: The bursting of the Tech Bubble led directly to the 2000-2002 bear market.
facts.claim: The tech bubble bursting caused the 2000-02 bear market.

facts.quote: The Global Financial Crisis created the 2007-2009 bear market as the housing market imploded.
facts.claim: The 2007-09 bear market came from the global financial crisis as housing collapsed.

facts.quote: This one is defined by the Fed tightening interest rates in reply to galloping inflation that's running at the fastest clip in 40 years
facts.claim: The 2022 bear market was driven by the Fed raising rates to fight the fastest inflation in 40 years.

facts.quote: The broad market index rose 1.23% to settle at 4,839.81, surpassing both the prior record intraday and closing highs from January 2022.
facts.claim: On January 19, 2024 the S&P 500 closed at a record 4,839.81, above its January 2022 records.

facts.quote: Friday's milestone confirms that the stock market is officially in a bull market that began in October 2022, and not just a bounce within a bear market.
facts.claim: CNBC, going by the record-high yardstick, said the January 2024 record confirmed a bull market that began in October 2022.

facts.quote: a case in point is the S&P 500's pandemic-fueled bear market in early 2020, which lasted a mere 33 days from the previous high on February 19 to the trough on March 23.
facts.claim: The S&P 500's 2020 fall took 33 days, from its February 19 high to its March 23 trough.

facts.quote: And they often end as abruptly as they began, with a quick rebound that is very difficult to predict
facts.claim: Bear markets often end abruptly, with a rebound that is very hard to predict.

facts.quote: 8. March 2000 to October 2002 Duration: 31 months S&P 500 loss: 49 percent The dot-com bubble burst was the main trigger for this bear market.
facts.claim: Fox Business (Ned Davis data): the S&P 500 lost 49% from March 2000 to October 2002, set off by the dot-com bubble bursting.

facts.quote: Broad equity price indexes were volatile and declined sharply, on net, amid sustained inflation pressures and expectations of monetary policy tightening, as well as heightened uncertainty regarding Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the economic outlook
facts.claim: In the first half of 2022 US stocks fell sharply on high inflation, expected Fed tightening and uncertainty over Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

facts.quote: Concerns over the sustainability of corporate earnings growth, the global growth outlook, international trade tensions, and some Federal Reserve communications that were perceived as less accommodative than expected weighed on investor sentiment for a time.
facts.claim: In late 2018, worries about earnings, global growth, trade tensions and the Fed weighed on US stocks.

facts.quote: Measures of implied and realized stock price volatility for the S&P 500 index--the VIX and the 20-day realized volatility--increased sharply in the fourth quarter of last year
facts.claim: S&P 500 volatility jumped in the fourth quarter of 2018, during the sharp fall in stock prices.

facts.quote: 9. October 2007 to March 2009 Duration: 17 months S&P 500 loss: 57 percent The collapse in the U.S. housing market triggered this bear market.
facts.claim: Fox Business (Ned Davis data): the S&P 500 lost 57% from October 2007 to March 2009, set off by the housing collapse.

walkthroughs.title: Four things to read in any fall
steps: Every big fall has a depth, a length, a cause and an aftermath. Read all four before you call it.
Depth: the S&P 500 fell 57% from its 2007 peak to its 2009 trough. From 2000 to 2002 it fell 49.1%.
Length: in 2020 the fall took 33 days. The slide from 2000 to 2002 ground on for 30.5 months.
Cause tells you what broke. Aftermath tells you how long the repair took.

walkthroughs.title: Stocks and the economy keep different clocks
steps: In 2009 the S&P 500 hit its trough in March. The recession didn't end until June.
In 2002 it ran the other way. The recession ended in November 2001, yet stocks slid to new lows by October 2002.
Both times, the official end date came out over a year later. By then, price had already moved.

walkthroughs.title: A bounce is not a bottom
steps: In 2022 the S&P 500 fell from a record 4,796.56 in January to 3,666.77 in mid-June.
Then it bounced for two months, up to 4,305.20 in mid-August.
By October 12 it closed at 3,577.03, a new low. Only in hindsight did that turn out to be the bottom.

questions.q: Since 2000, which fall cut the S&P 500 the most from peak to low?
questions.why: The 2007-09 financial crisis. The S&P 500 fell 57% from its October 2007 peak to its March 2009 trough, the deepest of the four.
questions.lesson_line: The worst of these falls took 57% off the index. Never assume a drop can't go that deep.

wrong.The 2000-02 dot-com bust: Close, but not the deepest. The S&P 500 fell 49.1% from March 2000 to October 2002.
wrong.The 2020 COVID shutdown crash: It was the fastest, not the deepest. The S&P 500 fell 33.9% from February 19 to March 23, 2020.
wrong.The 2022 inflation bear market: A smaller fall. The S&P 500 went from 4,796.56 in January 2022 to 3,577.03 in October.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The 2007-09 bear market grew out of a collapse in ___ prices.
questions.why: Home. Falling home prices helped spark the financial crisis of 2007-08. On average they fell about 30% from mid-2006 to mid-2009.
questions.lesson_line: 2007-09 started in housing, then spread through the banks to the whole market.

questions.q: After the September 11, 2001 attacks, the New York Stock Exchange stayed shut until the following Monday.
questions.why: True. NYSE trading did not resume until Monday, September 17. For days there was no NYSE trading at all.
questions.lesson_line: A market can close for days. Size every position so you can live with not getting out.

questions.q: What set off the 2000-02 bear market in US stocks?
choices: The US losing its AAA rating
questions.why: The dot-com bubble bursting. Investors grew worried about lofty valuations, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell hardest. The S&P 500 lost 49.1%.
questions.lesson_line: When the market's leaders trade at lofty prices, their fall can drag the whole market down for years.

wrong.A collapse in home prices: That was 2007-09. Falling home prices helped spark that crisis.
wrong.A pandemic shutting the economy: That was 2020, a fall that took weeks, not years.
wrong.The US losing its AAA rating: That came in 2011, when Standard & Poor's cut the US credit rating from AAA to AA+.

questions.q: When the index made this low, the recession had already ended.
questions.why: False. The S&P 500 hit its trough in March 2009, but the recession ran until June 2009. Stocks turned months before the economy did.
questions.lesson_line: In 2009 stocks turned while the recession was still on. Bad news alone doesn't tell you where the low is.

questions.q: What drove the 2022 bear market in US stocks?
choices: Hot inflation and Fed rate hikes
questions.answer: Hot inflation and Fed rate hikes
questions.why: Hot inflation and Fed rate hikes. Stocks fell amid sustained inflation and expected Fed tightening, and Russia's invasion of Ukraine added to the uncertainty.
questions.lesson_line: When the Fed raises rates to fight inflation, it can pull the whole market lower, not just a few stocks.

wrong.A collapse in home prices: That was 2007-09, when falling home prices helped spark the financial crisis.
wrong.A US credit rating downgrade: That was 2011, when Standard & Poor's cut the US credit rating from AAA to AA+.

questions.q: Since 2000, which big S&P 500 fall reached its low the fastest?
questions.why: The 2020 COVID crash. It took 33 days, from February 19 to March 23. The 2007-09 fall took 17 months, and 2000-02 took 30.5 months.
questions.lesson_line: Some falls take years, one took 33 days. Your risk plan has to handle both.

wrong.The 2007-09 financial crisis: That one took 17 months, from October 2007 to March 2009.
wrong.The 2000-02 dot-com bust: The slowest of the group: 30.5 months, from March 2000 to October 2002.
wrong.The 2022 inflation bear: It ran from January 3 to October 12, 2022, about nine months.

questions.q: The S&P 500 closed at a 2,930.75 peak in September 2018 and at 2,351.10 on December 24. How far did it fall, in %? One decimal.
questions.why: 19.8%. From 2,930.75 down to 2,351.10, on worries about earnings, global growth, trade and the Fed. It stopped just short of the 20% fall that generally marks a bear market.
questions.lesson_line: Measure from the closing peak. Late 2018 came within a hair of 20%, then turned.

questions.q: After this low, the index took years to close back above its old peak.
questions.why: False. The S&P 500 closed at 2,933.68 on April 23, 2019, above its 2,930.75 peak, about four months after its 2,351.10 low.
questions.lesson_line: Not every deep drop becomes a long bear. Some heal in months.

questions.q: What drove the sharp drop at the end of this chart?
choices: A collapse in US home prices
questions.why: The debt-limit fight and Europe's crisis. Stocks fell sharply on Europe's debt crisis, the US debt-ceiling fight and fears of slower growth. Standard & Poor's also cut the US credit rating to AA+.
questions.lesson_line: This scare healed. Stocks roughly won back those losses by early 2012.

wrong.A collapse in US home prices: That was 2007-09, when falling home prices helped spark the financial crisis.

questions.q: From its March 2000 peak, how long did the Nasdaq Composite take to close above that level again?
questions.why: About 15 years. It closed at 5,048.62 on March 10, 2000 and didn't close higher until April 23, 2015, at 5,056.06.
questions.lesson_line: After a bubble, the old leaders can take a decade or more to come back. Don't marry them.

wrong.About five months: Far too fast. The index didn't even hit its low until October 9, 2002, at 1,114.11.
wrong.About two years: Two years in, it was still falling. It closed at 1,114.11 on October 9, 2002.

questions.q: What weighed on US stocks through this choppy slide?
choices: A collapse in US home prices
The US losing its AAA rating
questions.why: China worries and falling oil. Worries about the economy abroad hit stocks, China's currency moves stirred global turmoil, and energy stocks fell with oil.
questions.lesson_line: Trouble abroad and a falling oil price can drag on US stocks for months.

wrong.A collapse in US home prices: That was 2007-09, when falling home prices helped spark the financial crisis.
wrong.The US losing its AAA rating: That was 2011, when Standard & Poor's cut the US credit rating from AAA to AA+.

questions.q: Nasdaq Composite: 5,048.62 at its March 2000 peak, 1,114.11 at its October 2002 low. How far did it fall? Nearest whole %.
questions.why: 78%. From 5,048.62 down to 1,114.11. The tech-heavy index lost more than three quarters of its value.
questions.lesson_line: The bubble's leaders fell hardest. The Nasdaq lost far more than the S&P 500's 49.1%.

questions.q: How long did this fall take, from the peak close to the last close shown?
questions.why: About nine months. The S&P 500 closed at its 4,796.56 peak on January 3, 2022, and at 3,577.03 on October 12.
questions.lesson_line: A slow bear grinds you down. I cut size early instead of waiting for one big flush.

wrong.About five weeks: That was the 2020 pace: 33 days from February 19 to March 23.
wrong.About seventeen months: That was 2007-09, from October 2007 to March 2009.

questions.story: Stock index futures hit their 5% limit down before the open. This fund opens 5.2% below Friday's close and is down 7.8% by 9:35. Your sell stop sits 6% below Friday's close.
questions.q: What happens to your stop order?
choices: It becomes a market order and sells
It fills at exactly your stop price
It waits for the price to recover
It cancels when trading turns wild
questions.answer: It becomes a market order and sells
questions.why: It becomes a market order and sells. A stop price is a trigger, not a promised fill. Your stop hit at 6% down, yet this fund closed down only 4.2%.
questions.lesson_line: A stop is a trigger, not a price. In a wild open it can sell you near the low.

wrong.It fills at exactly your stop price: No. The stop price is not a guaranteed fill. Once it triggers, it's a market order and takes the next prices available.
wrong.It waits for the price to recover: A stop doesn't wait. A short, sharp drop can trigger it, even if the price rebounds later.
wrong.It cancels when trading turns wild: A fast market doesn't cancel it. That's exactly when a stop can fill far from its price.

questions.story: The index fell hard for months. Then it bounced for two straight months off its low, a big rally.
questions.q: What did the index do next?
choices: Fell to a new low within two months
Went on to make a new record that year
Held its gains and went sideways
questions.answer: Fell to a new low within two months
questions.why: It fell to a new low. The S&P 500 rose from 3,666.77 on June 16 to 4,305.20 on August 16. Then it closed at 3,577.03 on October 12, below the June low.
questions.lesson_line: A big bounce inside a bear is not proof of a bottom. That only shows up in hindsight.

wrong.Went on to make a new record that year: No. The S&P 500's 4,796.56 record from January 2022 wasn't topped until January 2024.
wrong.Held its gains and went sideways: The S&P 500 gave the whole rally back and more, closing at 3,577.03 on October 12.

questions.q: The S&P 500 closed at 1,565.15 at its 2007 peak and 676.53 at its 2009 low. What gain gets it back to the peak? Nearest whole %.
questions.why: 131%. From 676.53 back up to 1,565.15. A 56.8% loss needs a 131% gain just to get back to even.
questions.lesson_line: Big losses need far bigger gains to repair. Cutting losses early is cheaper than climbing out.

questions.q: The official end date of a US recession is announced the same month the recession ends.
questions.why: False. The NBER named the November 2001 trough on July 17, 2003, June 2009 on September 20, 2010, and April 2020 on July 19, 2021.
questions.lesson_line: In 2001, 2009 and 2020 the official end date came over a year late. Trade what price is doing now.

questions.story: A friend says every big market fall looks like 2008: a slide of more than a year that cuts stocks in half.
questions.q: What does the record since 2000 say?
choices: Falls vary a lot in speed and depth
He's right, they all look like 2008
Every fall stops near a 20% drop
questions.answer: Falls vary a lot in speed and depth
questions.why: They vary a lot. 2020 took 33 days and fell 33.9%. 2000-02 took 30.5 months and fell 49.1%. 2007-09 fell 56.8% in 17 months.
questions.lesson_line: Don't plan for one kind of fall. Plan for fast and slow, shallow and deep.

wrong.He's right, they all look like 2008: 2000-02 and 2007-09 fit that. But the 2020 fall was over in 33 days.
wrong.Every fall stops near a 20% drop: Some stop near there. 2007-09 went on to 56.8%.

questions.story: The economy has been growing for most of a year. Accounting scandals and profit warnings keep hitting stocks. The index sits at a new low.
questions.q: What does this low teach you?
choices: Stocks can fall once a recession ends
Stocks bottom before the economy does
A growing economy stops a stock slide
questions.answer: Stocks can fall once a recession ends
questions.why: Stocks can fall once a recession ends. The recession ended in November 2001, yet by early October 2002 stocks were at their lowest since 1997.
questions.lesson_line: The economy and the market keep different clocks. Trade the chart, not the GDP headlines.

wrong.Stocks bottom before the economy does: Not always. In 2009 they did, but here the low came almost a year after the recession ended.
wrong.A growing economy stops a stock slide: It didn't here. The economy grew in 2002 while scandals and profit warnings drove stocks lower.

conflicts: Bear market definition: Investor.gov (f31) says 'Generally' a 20% fall 'over at least a two-month period'; S&P Dow Jones Indices (f43-f47, via CNBC) counts the 2020 fall of 1.1 months as a bear market, and its full table also lists 1990's -19.9% as one while leaving out late 2018's -19.8%. So no question keys whether 2020 or late 2018 'was a bear market'. Questions say 'fall', give the depth, and q08 says 2018 stopped 'just short of the 20% fall that generally marks a bear market'.

Charts show SPY, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF, split-adjusted; the facts quote the S&P 500 index. The fund's percent moves track the index closely but not exactly (dividends, fees), so every depth or price is given as the index's own close, and every chart question that quotes a level names the S&P 500 in its reveal. q08 works from index closes, so it carries no chart: a fund axis near 293 beside an index close of 2,930.75 would only confuse. The only fund numbers are q15's, and those are the SEC note's own SPY figures.

2000-02 depth and length: S&P DJI via CNBC (f44) says 49.1% over 30.5 months; Fox Business (f56, Ned Davis data) says 49 percent over 31 months. They agree within rounding; the file uses S&P DJI's 49.1% and 30.5 months. The Fox Business page (December 26, 2018) opens by saying the S&P 500 had entered bear market territory, which was true only intraday on December 24, 2018 (the close was down 19.8% from the peak, per FRED). Only its 2000-02 and 2007-09 rows are used, and each matches S&P DJI.

2007-09 depth: Federal Reserve History (f02) says 57 percent; S&P DJI (f45) says 56.8%. Same fall, rounded differently. The file says 57% where it cites the Fed and 56.8% where it cites S&P DJI or computes from 1,565.15 and 676.53.

'First close above' claims (f34 April 23, 2019; f39 January 19, 2024; f42 April 23, 2015) rest on the whole daily series at the cited FRED range URL, which starts before the peak and ends on the recovery day, so the checker can confirm no close in between was higher.
